idiom_name: static T& instance() { static T t; return t; }
implementation_notes: The C++11 language guarantee absorbed the pattern: initialisation of a block-scope static happens exactly once and is thread-safe, and implementations use variants of double-checked locking internally so an already-initialised static costs a single non-atomic flag comparison. Use it for a constructible, non-rebuildable cell; the classic hand-written double check is a regression here, not an optimisation.
code_sketch:
Config& config() {                       // one thread-safe initialisation
    static Config cfg = Config::load();  // C++11 guarantees it once
    return cfg;                          // then a single flag test
}
pitfalls: The guarantee covers construction only: at exit the destructor runs in an unspecified order relative to other statics and other threads, so a lazily built global destroyed during shutdown can still be read by a running thread.

If the initialiser throws, the exception propagates to the caller and the static is re-attempted on the next call (the standard's retry rule), so a partially constructed resource must never be published by the initialiser.
A function-local static is per function call site, not per object: per-instance laziness needs a member and therefore a different mechanism.
Recursive initialisation of the same static is undefined behaviour or a deadlock (the guard is non-reentrant), so the initialiser must not call the accessor again.

variants.name: std::call_once with std::once_flag
variants.idiom_name: std::call_once(flag, factory) for cells that cannot be block-scope statics
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library's once primitive: std::call_once runs the callable exactly once and blocks concurrent callers until it has finished, which is the right tool when the cell is a member, must be built with arguments, or must stay resettable through a wrapper. It replaces the flag-and-check structure with a named object and, unlike a magic static, lets the accessor decide what a failed build means.
pitfalls: std::once_flag is one-shot by definition: there is no reset, so re-initialisation needs a mutex plus an atomic snapshot rather than a second call_once.
Recursively calling call_once on the same flag deadlocks, and an exception thrown by the callable is rethrown to every caller while the flag stays unset (the call may run again).
The atomic fast path in front of call_once is optional: without it the accessor still pays a once-flag test, which is usually the honest choice unless profiling says otherwise.

variants.name: hand-written double check over std::atomic<T*>
variants.idiom_name: std::atomic<Cell*> with release store and acquire load plus a mutex for the slow path
variants.implementation_notes: The manual transformed form for cases where a block-scope static is impossible (the value lives in an object pool, must be rebuilt, or the code predates C++11): one atomic pointer carries both the reference and the ordering, so the fast path is a single acquire load and the slow path a mutex with a re-test. Keep it only when the platform's primitives cannot express the lifetime, and never with a plain pointer.
pitfalls: Relaxed loads on the fast path, or a plain pointer, remove the acquire and let readers observe the pointer before the object's contents - the exact failure the pattern is supposed to prevent.
Rebuilding after publication needs a lifetime strategy (hazard pointers, reference counting); swapping the pointer while readers hold it is a use-after-free, not a locking problem.
Holding the mutex while running an arbitrary initialiser invites re-entrancy deadlock if the constructor calls back into the accessor.
